title: Puranmashi, the full moon
hook: full-moon gatherings recall Guru Nanak's birth at the Katak full moon

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sangrand, and your line: the month begins. Did you mark the next first-of-the-month in your calendar? The sun sets the Punjabi months. Today, the moon gets its turn. Day six hundred eighty-two.

Once a month it happens on the way to the car or out with the trash: the full moon, huge and low and orange over the rooftops. People stop. They take bad phone photos of it. They text someone, did you see the moon? Strangers on the same sidewalk point it out to each other. For a minute, the sky is the news. In Sikh communities, that night has a name, and in many places, a gathering. Today: Puranmashi.
screen: `ONCE A MONTH, PEOPLE LOOK UP.` → `BAD PHONE PHOTOS OF THE MOON.` → `A NIGHT WITH A NAME.`

segments.voice: Puranmashi means the full-moon day. Many gurdwaras hold a special diwan on the full moon each month, with kirtan, katha and langar, sometimes running late into the evening. Why the full moon? The reason Sikhs give is Guru Nanak. His birth, his gurpurab, is celebrated on the full moon of the month of Katak, in October or November. On that night, gurdwaras are lit up, processions fill the streets in the days before, and an unbroken reading of the Guru Granth Sahib often ends that morning. So each month's full moon carries a small echo of that one. Historians add a detail worth knowing. Some early accounts of Guru Nanak's life give his birth in the spring month of Vaisakh, not Katak. The Katak full moon is the long-standing tradition. The sources disagree, and Sikhs have kept the Katak celebration. The moon also shines inside the Granth. In Guru Nanak's Aarti, on Ang six sixty-three, the whole sky is pictured as a platter for worship, with the sun and the moon as its lamps. In paraphrase: the sky is the plate, the sun and moon the lamps, the stars the pearls. The full moon, in that picture, isn't a symbol of anything you have to explain. It's simply one of the lamps the universe holds up to its Creator, and you get to see it.
screen: `PURANMASHI: THE FULL MOON.` · `GURU NANAK'S KATAK FULL MOON.` · `SOURCES DIFFER ON THE DATE.` · `THE MOON AS A LAMP IN THE AARTI.` · then, large: `FULL MOON, FULL HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at the moon. If it's night and you can see it, go to a window or step outside and look. If it's day, or cloudy, picture the last full moon you remember. Let it be a lamp held up in a huge silent room. Breathe slowly while you look. Think of how many people across the world are under the same moon tonight. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, as one more voice in that room. The bell holds the time.
Puranmashi. The full moon, when many gurdwaras gather, echoing Guru Nanak's gurpurab on the full moon of Katak.
Your line: full moon, full heart. Tonight or at the next full moon, look up for one minute and send the sight to someone you love. Day six hundred eighty-two.
